item.title: Durga Puja begins Friday in Bangladesh
item.description:
Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community, will begin in Bangladesh on Friday with Maha Shasthi.
On the first day, devotees will perform Bodhan, the ceremonial awakening and invocation of Goddess Durga, marking the formal commencement of the festivities.
This year, Durga Puja will be celebrated at 33,165 mandaps across the country.
Devotees of all ages are expected to visit the mandaps and offer prayers to Goddess Durga, seeking divine blessings for peace, prosperity and the welfare of the country and its people.
Mahalaya, which marks the beginning of preparations for Durga Puja, was observed across the country on October 9. It is associated with the ceremonial invocation of Goddess Durga and is observed seven days before the festival begins.
The main rituals will continue through Bijoya Dashami on October 21, when devotees bid farewell to the goddess. The festival will conclude with the immersion of idols.
This year, Maha Saptami Puja will be celebrated for two days on Saturday and Sunday, Maha Ashtami on Monday, Maha Nabami on Tuesday.
Adequate security measures have been taken to ensure peaceful celebrations, with members of different law enforcement agencies deployed at puja mandaps across the country.
A total of 212,118 members of the Bangladesh Ansar and Village Defence Party have been deployed for security during the festival, with eight members assigned to each high-risk mandap and six to each of the other mandaps.
Besides, 104 striking teams will remain on standby to respond quickly to any untoward incident, said its Director General Major General Abdul Motaleb Sazzad Mahmud at a press conference at its headquarters on Thursday.
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) is also setting up 18 base camps and strengthening patrols to ensure security at around 1,800 puja mandaps located within eight kilometres of the country's borders during Durga Puja.
BGB Director General Major General Mohammad Ashrafuzzaman Siddiqui disclosed the plan while talking to reporters after inspecting the security arrangements at the Ramna Kali Mandir in the capital on Thursday afternoon.
He said BGB personnel have already visited the mandaps and contacted puja committees in their respective areas to coordinate security measures.
The government has declared a three-day holiday on the occasion of Durga Puja from October 20 to 22.
With October 23 and 24 falling on Friday and Saturday, the regular weekly holidays, there will be a five-day vacation from October 20 to 24.

item.title: NCP vows to raise voice on religious discrimination
item.description:
National Citizen Party (NCP) Convener Nahid Islam on Thursday said his party will raise cases of religious discrimination in Parliament and take to the streets on the issue whenever such incidents come to its attention.
He made the remarks while addressing a press briefing following a meeting with Hindu community leaders ahead of Durga Puja at the party’s central office in the city.
Nahid said ensuring equal dignity for citizens regardless of their religious or ethnic identities is central to the NCP’s political philosophy.
The NCP has instructed its leaders and activists across the country to extend all possible assistance to members of the Hindu community in celebrating Durga Puja, he said.
The party will also provide voluntary support for the celebrations, and take part in festivities at different locations, within its capacity, Nahid added.
He said the goal should be to build a Bangladesh where religious communities celebrate their festivals without having to worry about security.
Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad General Secretary Santosh Sharma alleged that the Hindu community had faced discrimination in government jobs, businesses and other areas since August 5, 2024, and urged NCP leaders to raise the issue in Parliament.
He also alleged that members of the community had faced intimidation, extortion and land grabbing.
The NCP leader said political parties should maintain good relations with all religious and ethnic communities and play a role in protecting their rights.
He also called on all to act responsibly to maintain communal harmony, warning that various forces might seek to undermine it.
Leaders of the Bangladesh Puja Udjapan Parishad and the Bangladesh Hindu Buddhist Christian Oikya Parishad attended the meeting and exchanged greetings with NCP leaders.

item.title: Sajek reopens to tourists, road blockade suspended for puja
item.description:
Sajek Valley, a popular tourist destination in Rangamati’s Baghaichhari upazila, has reopened to visitors, while two local organisations have suspended their road blockade program for six days, from October 16 to 21, to allow celebrations of Durga Puja.
The Rangamati district administration announced the reopening in an emergency public notice issued from the deputy commissioner’s office at 8pm on Thursday.
Earlier that afternoon, the Sajek Karbari Association and the Sajek Gono Odhikar Rokkha Committee announced the suspension of the blockade in a press release sent to the media.
The public notice, signed by District Magistrate Nazma Ashrafi, said tourist destinations, including Sajek Valley, had been reopened following a revision of the instructions issued in an emergency notice on October 11.
The district administration had earlier suspended tourist visits to Sajek Valley from 6pm on October 11 until further notice, citing unavoidable circumstances and concerns over visitor safety.
Meanwhile, the Sajek Karbari Association and the Sajek Gono Odhikar Rokkha Committee decided to suspend their road blockade during Durga Puja, following a request from the Sajek Machalong Bazar Durga Puja Celebration Committee.
Durga Puja will also be celebrated at Machalong Bazar in Sajek. The organisations said the temporary suspension was intended to ensure that the religious festival could be observed with due dignity and respect.
Sajek Karbari Association President Notun Joy Chakma and Sajek Gon Odhikar Rokkha Committee Convener Babudhan Chakma confirmed the decision in the statement.
The leaders said their program was not influenced by any political party and was not directed against people of any ethnicity, religion or caste. Rather, they said, it had been called to demand the safety of Sajek residents and the protection of their lives and property.
They warned that the road blockade would resume after the Durga Puja celebrations if the administration failed to meet the residents’ demands. Details of the next programme would be announced through a press release in due course, they added.
The leaders also urged the administration to take prompt and effective steps to ensure peace in the area by implementing the residents’ three-point set of demands and conditions.

item.title: Expatriates take alternative routes to Riyadh despite extra costs, risks
item.description:
Mamun, a resident of Noakhali Sadar, works as a truck driver for a company in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. After living abroad for five years, he returned to Bangladesh for the first time two months ago.
His return flight to Riyadh was scheduled for October 11, but it was cancelled. He booked another ticket for October 12, only for that flight to be cancelled as well.
With just five days left on his visa, Mamun grew increasingly worried. He finally secured a ticket for a flight to Medina on October 15.
Despite fears over the ongoing conflict, he is relieved to be able to return to Saudi Arabia.
Speaking at Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport’s (HSIA) departure terminal, Mamun said: “My visa is about to expire, but I could not leave. I was extremely worried. Finally, I can travel via Medina.”
However, the alternative route means more time, expense and hassle. From Medina, he will have to travel by bus for 12 to 14 hours to reach Riyadh.
“We have already faced so much trouble, and now there is more waiting for us in Medina. Travelling from there to Riyadh will take 12 to 14 hours by bus, with additional expenses. But we have no choice. We have to go, so we are accepting the extra costs and risks. Please pray for us,” he said.
Parvez, an expatriate worker from Manikganj, has faced similar difficulties following repeated flight cancellations.
“We have been through a lot of hassle. One flight after another was cancelled, and I thought I would not be able to travel at all. Now I have to go via Medina,” he said.
With around seven days remaining on his visa, Parvez decided to travel rather than risk further delays.
“I know there are security concerns, but we have no choice. We have to go,” he said.
Al Amin, from Nabinagar in Brahmanbaria, said flights to Riyadh and Dammam had been cancelled, leaving passengers uncertain about when services would resume.
“All flights to Riyadh and Dammam have been cancelled, and nobody knows when they will resume. Our visas are also about to expire. What are we supposed to do? We are being forced to travel via Medina and then take a bus to Riyadh, which will take around 14 hours,” he said.
“If we could fly directly, we would not have to go through all this trouble. But what can we do? We have no other option if we want to keep our jobs,” he added.
A visit to the airport found expatriate workers travelling to Riyadh via Medina, with many whose visas were nearing expiry changing their tickets to take the alternative route.
The Biman Bangladesh Airlines flight to Medina was scheduled to depart at 3:55pm, and passengers began arriving at the airport by noon. As they prepared to board, their earlier anxiety gave way to relief at finally being able to travel.
Passengers said they had to make repeated trips from their villages to change their tickets. The alternative route and additional travel expenses were costing them an extra Tk20,000-25,000.
Despite the added costs and security concerns, many were relieved to be able to leave Bangladesh before their visas expired.
On October 10, Riyadh airport came under attack by Yemen’s Houthi rebels. Dammam airport was subsequently targeted by a missile, disrupting flight operations.
By Thursday, over 100 flights had been cancelled from HSIA, leaving more than 15,000 expatriate Bangladeshis stranded.

item.title: Feed Industry in trouble as prices of raw materials increase
item.description:
Prices of different raw materials used in poultry feed recently increased by 9% to 40%. In response, feed manufacturers have raised the prices of their products by a meagre 7%. Many are not recovering the cost of production. Rising global prices of raw materials have resulted in margins being squeezed.
However, some critics have been quick to allege that the increase in feed price has no rationale other than profit maximisation. They claim that the price increase has harmed farmers, and increased the prices of chicken and eggs.
Poultry feed manufacturers argue that the price increases are not enough to conver their increased costs. As the industry is very competitive, each feed company is afraid that increasing its price will lead to a loss of market share. Because competition is intense, the feed industry operates with a very thin profit margin.
According to the late September 2026 data, the price of maize increased from Tk31.3 to Tk38.8 (per kg), soya bean meal from Tk58 to Tk66 (per kg). Maize and soya bean meal are the major ingredients of poultry feed. Though the price of maize increased by 24% and the price of soya bean meal increased by 14%, the price of poultry feed was raised only 7%, from Tk68 per kg to Tk72.50 per kg.
Other feed materials have also become more expensive. De-oiled rice bran from Tk26 to Tk33 (per kg), rice bran from Tk33 to Tk39 (per kg), and mustard oil cake from Tk36.50 to Tk39.70 (per kg).
The increasing cost of poultry feed inevitably increases the prices of chicken and eggs. Poultry industry stakeholders suggest reducing taxes on the industry to arrest the upward price spiral.
Mosharaf Hossain Chowdhury, president of Bangladesh Poultry Industries Association (BPIA) and managing director of Asta Feed Mill, mentioned that the price of soya bean meal rose 20% or $100 to $530 (per ton) in the international market in August. “The price of feed was increased by Tk2 per kg in late August and Tk2.50 per kg in September. Yet, feed mill owners are making losses,” he argued.
The first increase in raw material prices came when the maize price increased in Brazil and the shipping cost also went up. Moshiur Rahman, managing director of Paragon Agro Industries, said: “Raw material price increase elsewhere or supply disruption immediately affects the Bangladesh market.”
Ihtesham B Shahjahan, managing director of Quality Feeds Limited explained that it requires almost 80 ingredients to prepare poultry feeds and their prices increased by up to 40%.
BPIA leaders told this author that in the budget for fiscal year 2025-26, the rate of corporate income tax for the poultry sector increased from 15% to 27.5%. As a result, the net profit has already become very low, and feed mills must pass cost increases on to farmers.
ATM Habibur Rahman, chief commercial officer of Akij Feed Mill, said that the price of maize recently increased from $235 to $290 per ton. “If prices of all ingredients increase, how can we sell the poultry feed at same price?” he questioned.
Md Anwarul Haque, general secretary of Feed Industries Association of Bangladesh and managing director of Padma Feed Mill, pointed out that the poultry feed industry is imports 65% of its raw materials. “The prices of feeds have been raised only slightly, in comparison to the increases in prices of raw materials. We are in a survival mode now,” he added.
A recent Bangladesh Bank report reviewed the cost structure of a few companies, and calculated the cost of production of broiler grower feed at Tk61.77 per kg, and sales price at Tk69.75 per kg.
Around 150 companies produce 7.5 million tons of animal feeds, 70% of which is consumed by the poultry sector. A large number of informal feed mills also produce an additional volume of feed.
A study by Bangladesh Agriculture University predicted that the demand for animal feed will increase to 10 million tons by 2030 and that the poultry sector will account for 65% of it.

item.title: School bus runs over 8-year-old at Adamjee Cantonment School
item.description:
An eight-year-old student of Adamjee Cantonment Public School and College died after being run over by a bus on the compound of the institution’s Jalshiri branch in Rupganj, Narayanganj, on Tuesday.
The deceased, Shahriar Shayan, was the son of Saju Ahmed, a resident of the Batatola area of Khilkhet in Dhaka. He was a second-grade student.
The death has raised concerns among guardians about student safety and the school’s transport arrangements, prompting demands for stricter safety measures.
Rupganj Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) AHM Salauddin told Dhaka Tribune on Thursday morning that the student had died after being run over by a bus.
“On receiving the news, a police team went to the spot. After inspecting the scene, we spoke with the student’s guardians. We offered them every kind of legal assistance,” he said.
The OC said police had urged the family to file a case and assured them of legal assistance.
“We told them, ‘We are by your side. File a case. You will be given every kind of legal assistance,’” he said.
However, Shayan’s father, Saju Ahmed Selim, declined to file a case.
“Who would I file a case for? The one I would file it for is already gone,” he said.
The OC added that no one had lodged a complaint over the incident.
Saidur Rahman, a retired warrant officer and the school’s senior office superintendent, told Dhaka Tribune on Thursday morning that Shayan was standing behind a school bus while preparing to go home after classes ended.
The bus ran over the child while reversing, killing him on the spot, Rahman said.
“This is an unfortunate incident, and we are mourning. A four-member committee, headed by the school principal, has been formed to investigate the incident. An inquiry into compensation for the child’s family is also underway,” he said.
Rahman added that the bus company and the driver would be changed following the incident.
Following Shayan’s death, several guardians met with the principal and presented six demands to the school authorities.
According to guardians who attended the meeting, Principal Lt Col (retd) Muhammad Ferdous Hasan Titu said the authorities would begin implementing the demands in phases immediately after the upcoming Puja holidays.
The demands include establishing a designated area for students to safely get on and off school buses, away from regular traffic and other people; allowing guardians to accompany children from Nursery to class II on school buses; and barring outside vehicles from entering the campus.
The guardians also demanded that each bus maintain an attendance record and ensure students board and get off at designated stops in accordance with a student list.
They called for bus departures to be announced over a loudspeaker, saying buses are often delayed after classes end, leaving students waiting and playing on the school field.
Their final demand was that bus drivers and helpers be recruited only after undergoing drug tests.
Dhaka Tribune contacted Principal Titu for comment, but he did not respond to queries.
However, according to people familiar with the meeting, he acknowledged the school’s responsibility, saying: “We cannot escape this responsibility. We have formed an investigation committee to find out why such an incident occurred. The guilty will be identified and exemplary punishment will be ensured. The school authorities will remain vigilant so that such incidents do not happen in the future.”
Several guardians expressed concern about the safety of other children following Shayan’s death.
They said the school authorities could not evade responsibility, as the incident occurred on campus.
Shayan’s father, Saju Ahmed Selim, works at a private company and lives in the Batatola area of Khilkhet in Dhaka. His wife, Sharmin Khatun, is a homemaker.
Shayan was the elder of their two children. His younger sister, Shahrin, is 4 years old.
Selim told Dhaka Tribune that Shayan’s classes ended at 3pm every day and the school bus usually left between 3:15pm and 3:20pm.
“I was at my office in Dhanmondi at the time. The school called me at 3:40pm and asked me to come to the school urgently. I reached the school within 40 minutes by motorcycle. What I saw there, I was not prepared to see. My son Shayan was lying bloodied under the bus, in his school uniform with his ID card hanging around his neck. My world went dark,” he said.
Police and army personnel were also present at the scene, he said. After completing the legal procedures, he received his son’s body. The school later returned the child’s schoolbag and uniform.
Selim said he reviewed the school’s closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage with the principal’s help.
“It shows a bus leaving the campus, but there was no assistant on the bus. My son was probably playing at the time. As the bus took a left turn, my boy was crushed under the left wheel,” he said.
He questioned how such an incident could occur at an educational institution with around 20 buses and several thousand students.
“Such a big educational institution, around 20 buses and several thousand students. Such a great negligence cannot be accepted. The driver was driving inside the campus without an assistant, even though thousands of children are there. How was the driver driving without being careful even once? There is negligence on the part of the school authorities and the bus driver here,” he said.
Selim said he did not want to pursue a legal case because of the prospect of an autopsy, the time required to pursue the case and his work commitments. He also said he had no faith in the country’s legal system.
“My son’s body would have been cut open for an autopsy; there is the hassle of pursuing a case, I have a job, I lack time. Considering everything, I do not want to get entangled in legal trouble. Also, I have no faith in the country’s laws. So, I took my child’s body after giving a written statement,” he said.
However, he said he had demanded in the written statement that the school authorities investigate the incident and take disciplinary action against those involved.

item.title: Rising food prices force Dhaka families to cut back on nutrition
item.description:
Nasima Begum, a 45-year-old housewife in Dhaka, stood in a long queue at a subsidised food sale in Basabo, hoping to buy rice and other essentials at affordable prices.
“But even getting the subsidised goods is a struggle,” she said, describing overcrowding, pushing and long waits that sometimes end without people getting what they came for.
Nasima, who lives with her husband and three children, has had to change her family's eating habits to cope with rising prices. “We used to manage fish or meat at least once a month, but now even that is difficult,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
A few kilometres away in Malibagh, rickshaw puller Ripon Mia faces a similar squeeze.
Supporting a family of four, he now often settles for tea and ruti at a roadside tea stall for lunch instead of a meal of rice and an egg.
“I used to eat rice with an egg and sometimes vegetables, but even that is no longer affordable on my current income,” he said. “I cannot raise fares to offset the rising costs because passengers object. After meeting household expenses, little is left for food,” he added.
The strain is evident in the quantities people buy and the meals they choose, both at home and outside.
At Jatrabari, retailer Md Mintu said customers were buying smaller quantities of essential goods.
Some who previously bought five litres of cooking oil now buy only two, while those who bought a litre settle for half. The price of flour at his shop has risen from around Tk50 a kilogram a month ago to Tk65–70.
“Income is low compared with the prices of goods. People are feeling the strain,” he said.
Pickup driver Md Jashim's family now buys only what it needs immediately, adopting a bare-minimum approach to daily living.
Jashim recently spent about an hour in a queue at a subsidised food sale in Shahjahanpur to buy essential food grains. His wife now works in neighbouring households, earning an additional Tk3,000 a month on top of his monthly income of Tk15,000–20,000.
“Even with that extra income, we have to calculate every expense before spending because of the rising cost of living,” he said.
Restaurants are feeling the impact as well. Mohammad Kabir, who runs a restaurant in Rampura, said customers who once ordered meat were switching to vegetables, while some who previously ordered kebabs and roti were settling for a single Mughlai paratha. “Nowadays, for many lower-middle-income people, eating at a restaurant has become a luxury,” he said.
According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS), general inflation rose to 8.34% in September from 8.26% in August, while food inflation increased to 7.22% from 7.02%.
The national wage rate index grew by 7.90%, falling short of general inflation. This suggests that wage growth is not fully keeping pace with rising prices, although the effects vary across households.
Higher fuel prices have added to the pressure. On September 21, the government raised the prices of diesel, petrol, octane and kerosene by Tk20 per litre. Traders have cited higher transport costs and paddy prices as factors behind recent increases in rice prices.
During visits to several Dhaka markets this week, a Dhaka Tribune reporter found fine rice selling at Tk74–75 a kilogram, up from Tk72 a week earlier. Medium-grain rice was priced at Tk58–65, compared with Tk55–62 previously, while coarse rice remained at Tk50–55.
Eggs were selling at Tk155–160 a dozen, up from Tk130–135 a year earlier. Broiler chicken cost Tk180–200 a kilogram, while beef was priced at Tk780–800.
However, Trading Corporation of Bangladesh (TCB) data showed no weekly increase in rice prices and a decline in the price of fine rice. TCB Assistant Director Shatadal Mondal said the agency would examine the discrepancy.
Salaried households are also struggling as food, housing and transport costs rise simultaneously.
Mehedi Hasan Sohel, who works for a private organisation in Karwan Bazar, now earns Tk35,000 a month, up from Tk30,000 last year.
However, his family's monthly food expenses have risen from Tk12,000 to Tk15,000, absorbing Tk3,000 of his Tk5,000 salary increase.
His transport costs have also increased, as overcrowded buses sometimes force him to take a motorcycle or a CNG-powered auto-rickshaw.
Sabbir Rahman, an employee of a private company in Savar, has been struggling with debt for about a year.
“I don't know how, but somehow, prices and my salary are worlds apart. I cannot make my income match the cost of living. If I buy one thing, I cannot buy another,” he said.
Professor Selim Raihan, executive director of the South Asian Network on Economic Modeling (SANEM), said persistent inflation was putting substantial pressure on purchasing power, particularly among low- and lower-middle-income households.
Even where nominal wages have increased, he said, they often fail to keep pace with the cumulative rise in food, housing, transport and energy costs.
“As a result, many households are cutting food consumption, compromising dietary quality, postponing healthcare and education spending, or drawing down savings and taking on debt,” he added.
Nazneen Ahmed, executive director of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said the Open Market Sale (OMS) programme supports vulnerable households struggling with high prices.
“In view of inflation, food distribution should have been increased. But we see the opposite,” she said.
Md Moniruzzaman, director of the Procurement Division at the Directorate General of Food, said the government had around 1.964 million tonnes of rice and 310,000 tonnes of wheat in stock. Including floating stocks, total reserves stood at approximately 2.3 million tonnes.
However, he and Md Abdus Salam, director of the Supply, Distribution and Marketing Division, could not provide current figures on food distribution or details of the procedures involved.
Experts say food stocks indicate the country's supply capacity but do not necessarily reflect whether households can afford food or how much reaches consumers through subsidised programmes.
The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), citing an analysis by the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), projected that 18.1 million people in Bangladesh could face high levels of acute food insecurity between September and December 2026, up from 15.3 million during May–August.
Of them, around 787,000 people were projected to face emergency-level food insecurity.
Nutrition specialist Dr Md Shohag warned that when households replace eggs, fish and meat with diets dominated by rice and flour, they may continue to receive enough calories but fail to meet their protein and micronutrient requirements.
“Such deficiencies can hamper children's development and reduce adults' working capacity and resistance to disease,” he said.

item.title: Mob killed Shamim after dragging him from hospital; alleged instigator still free
item.description:
A man who publicly acknowledged mobilising people through Facebook ahead of the mob killing of Wahiduzzaman Shamim over allegations of blasphemy in Satkhira’s Debhata remains unarrested, even as police investigate the brutal attack in which the victim was dragged from a health facility and beaten to death.
Fazlul Haque Amini, identified by the victim’s family as a key instigator, has continued posting on social media and openly challenged the authorities to take action against him.
He has acknowledged using Facebook posts and live broadcasts to gather people over allegations that Shamim made derogatory remarks about Islam. However, his precise role in the fatal assault remains under investigation.
Debhata police said they were examining the social media posts and videos, along with CCTV footage, to identify those involved in the killing.
The incident has sparked outrage over the apparent failure to prevent repeated attacks on Shamim, who was reportedly rescued by police and taken to a health facility before being assaulted again.
Shamim’s family said he had been receiving treatment for mental health problems for years and was targeted after audio recordings of remarks made during a domestic dispute circulated online.
Amini began posting videos on his personal Facebook account from around 3:30pm on Tuesday, urging people to mobilise over allegations that Shamim had insulted Islam.
In some videos, he was seen calling on people to take action, while others showed him leading a procession.
Amini subsequently acknowledged that he had used Facebook posts and live broadcasts to gather people.
He also declared that he was prepared to face arrest, imprisonment or even the death penalty for his actions.
In statements circulated online, Amini argued that Shamim’s alleged remarks could not be excused on mental health grounds.
He claimed Shamim had repeatedly made offensive comments about Islam and said he considered protesting such remarks a religious obligation.
Amini also stated that he was not affiliated with any political party.
According to the account, he posted a photograph of Shamim after his death and expressed jubilation. He continued posting on Thursday, including material related to the audio recording at the centre of the allegations.
His activities have raised questions about why he had not been taken into custody despite publicly acknowledging his role in mobilising people.
Debhata Police Station Officer-in-Charge HM Shahin told media that police were aware of the Facebook posts and broadcasts.
“These matters have come to our attention. We are conducting our own operations and are taking action,” he said.
Police said investigators were examining CCTV footage from the hospital and surrounding areas, along with videos circulating on social media, to identify others involved.
According to Shamim’s family, the violence began on Monday following an argument between him and his wife.
His younger brother, Tawsif Rahman Sagar, said neighbours recorded remarks made during the dispute and circulated the audio on social media, accompanied by allegations of blasphemy.
A mob subsequently attacked the family’s home and vandalised property.
Shamim was also assaulted near Subarnabad market, according to his elder brother, Abdul Jalil.
Following the attack, Shamim returned home and consumed poison, his family said.
He was taken to the chamber of a local physician, MA Sabur, in the Kuliya area, where he received treatment and was kept under observation.
On Tuesday, a mob entered the doctor’s chamber and attacked him again.
Police intervened, rescued Shamim and took him to Sakhipur Health Complex.
However, the violence did not end there.
According to the family, another large mob entered the health facility, assaulted Shamim and dragged him outside.
Jalil alleged that Amini led the crowd, which he estimated numbered more than 1,000 people.
The attackers allegedly slammed Shamim against a wall and beat him severely.
Police subsequently recovered him and transferred him to Satkhira Medical College Hospital, where doctors declared him dead.
OC Shahin confirmed that Shamim had been attacked again after police initially rescued him.
“At 8:30pm, an agitated mob, or ‘Tawhidi Janata’, whatever one might call them, arrived and assaulted him again,” he said.
Shamim’s family described the killing as deliberate and demanded action against those responsible for mobilising the crowd.
“They incited people against him using a provocative video/audio clip, and then deliberately and systematically beat him to death,” Sagar said.
Sagar said his brother had completed his Honours and Master’s degrees in History at Jagannath University.
According to the family, Shamim developed mental health problems after being drugged by criminals during a bus journey several years ago.
He had experienced periods of mental instability for around a decade and had been receiving medical treatment.
The family said his condition had affected his personal life, including his first marriage.
Shamim leaves behind two sons, one from each marriage.
Sagar questioned why his brother had been subjected to mob violence instead of being dealt with through the legal system.
“If the law had punished him, we would have accepted it. But why should my brother be beaten to death without any trial?” he said.
The victim’s family also alleged that local Jamaat-e-Islami activists were involved in mobilising people during the initial attack.
Sagar claimed that some participants had gathered at a local Jamaat office before proceeding to the family’s home.
He alleged that local party leaders and activists were among those involved.
However, Kamrul Islam Gazi, president of the Ward 8 Jamaat-e-Islami unit in Parulia Union, denied the allegations.
He told BBC Bangla that local residents, rather than Jamaat activists, had assaulted Shamim.
“No... it was the local residents,” he said when asked whether party members were involved.
Gazi said he had heard that Shamim was beaten after being taken for treatment following his consumption of poison.
The family’s allegations against Jamaat members have not been independently established.
As of 3pm on Thursday, no murder case had been filed, according to police.
OC Shahin said police had contacted the victim’s family and were expecting them to visit the police station to lodge a complaint.
Sagar also said the family intended to file a case later in the day.
Police said the investigation was continuing and that legal action would be taken against those identified as responsible.

item.title: What’s going on with cow slaughter at Jagannath University?
item.description:
A dispute over cooking beef khichuri near a temple at Jagannath University has escalated into a controversy over religious sensitivities, the right to organise events on campus and the university administration’s handling of the situation.
What began on Monday as a dinner organized by students of the Department of Islamic History and Culture has now led to protests, conflicting interpretations of the incident, two administrative notices and plans for another event involving cow slaughter.
The university initially asked students to refrain from slaughtering animals on campus, citing public health and cleanliness.
However, following objections, it clarified that students had the right to organize such events, provided they did not interfere with others.
A group of students has since announced plans for a beef feast, while representatives of the university’s central temple say they have no objection to such an event as long as it does not take place in front of the temple or disrupt religious activities.
So, how did the controversy begin, and why has it continued despite attempts to resolve it?
On the evening of Monday, students from the 17th batch of Jagannath University’s Department of Islamic History and Culture organized a beef khichuri cookout near the campus’s Muktamancha.
The university’s central temple is situated nearby.
Some Hindu students objected to the location of the cooking arrangements, saying that preparing beef so close to the temple hurt their religious sentiments.
According to BBC Bangla, Joy Saha, member secretary of the university’s Central Temple Management Committee, approached the organizers with several other students around 8pm.
He said they asked what kind of meat was being cooked and eventually learned that it was beef.
“Given that it was happening in front of the temple, we felt quite distressed; our religious sentiments were hurt. We asked them to move it elsewhere,” he told BBC Bangla.
A heated exchange followed, with Saha alleging that some organizers responded provocatively and questioned the boundaries of the temple.
The university proctor intervened, and the cooking arrangements were moved farther away.
The organizers maintained that they had no intention of hurting anyone’s religious sentiments.
Another disagreement emerged over bricks allegedly taken from the temple premises to construct a temporary cooking stove.
According to The Daily Star, the organizers initially planned to cook at the university cafeteria but moved to an outdoor location because of low gas pressure.
They used bricks found nearby to build a stove, apparently without knowing that the bricks belonged to the temple.
After objections were raised, they said they removed the bricks, brought an iron stove from the cafeteria and apologised for the misunderstanding.
Some students consequently argued that the controversy was primarily about the use of temple property rather than the cooking of beef itself.
Joy Saha, however, disputed that interpretation.
He told BBC Bangla that the proximity of the cooking arrangements to the temple was the main concern, and the issue of bricks was secondary.
Following the confrontation, Hindu students held a procession on campus. The matter subsequently spread across social media, generating arguments between students and drawing wider attention.
According to the university administration, the initial disagreement was resolved on the spot through the proctor’s intervention.
Further discussions between the parties the following day helped settle the matter.
However, online arguments continued, with some students portraying the objections as an attempt to restrict their freedom to eat beef on campus.
Others maintained that the concern was not about what students could eat but about respecting the religious space surrounding the temple.
Amid the controversy, some students began discussing plans for a larger beef feast involving the slaughter of cows on campus.
That prompted the university administration to intervene again.
On Wednesday, the university issued a notice signed by Proctor Professor Dr Md Azam Khan, asking students, teachers, officers and employees to refrain from slaughtering animals on campus.
The notice cited public health, cleanliness and the need to maintain a hygienic environment.
It also referred to a Dhaka South City Corporation public notice concerning restrictions on animal slaughter and warned that violations could lead to legal action.
The directive triggered fresh objections from students who questioned why the university was restricting animal slaughter following the dispute over beef khichuri.
Professor Azam Khan told BBC Bangla that the intention was to prevent further tensions during religious observances, not to create another controversy.
He said the administration had learned of plans to slaughter an animal and wanted to avoid an undesirable situation.
Later on Wednesday, the administration issued another statement clarifying its position.
It said the original misunderstanding over the cookout had already been resolved and that its subsequent appeal against animal slaughter was intended to prevent fresh tensions and protect religious harmony.
Expressing regret over the misunderstanding caused by its earlier notice, the administration said everyone had the right to organise events on campus, including those involving animal slaughter.
However, it urged students to ensure that their activities did not obstruct or interfere with others.
The clarification effectively softened the administration’s earlier position.
It did not, however, establish whether any proposed slaughter would separately comply with applicable municipal regulations.
Despite the clarification, a group of students has announced plans for a larger beef feast on campus.
Organisers have collected contributions from students and purchased a cow. Bangladesh Chhatra Majlish has also reportedly pledged to provide another.
Social media announcements advertised a registration fee of Tk70 per participant.
An organizer told BBC Bangla that the event was being arranged in protest against the administration’s earlier restriction.
The organiser indicated that the cows would likely be slaughtered in an open field near the Arts Building rather than outside the temple.
Jagannath University Central Students’ Union General Secretary Abdul Alim Arif told BBC Bangla that student representatives had met the administration and reached an understanding allowing the program to proceed.
He described the planned event as a protest against the university’s decision.
The draft identifies Friday, as the planned date.
Representatives of the central temple have clarified that they are not demanding a blanket prohibition on beef consumption or cow slaughter on campus.
Their principal concern is the location and its potential effect on religious activities.
“If they want to slaughter cows on campus, let them, that’s not an issue,” Joy Saha told BBC Bangla.
“However, it must not happen in front of the temple, nor should it disrupt the order and sanctity of the temple premises.”
He emphasized that the number of cows was not the issue, provided the activities respected the temple and its surroundings.
The university administration has urged all parties to maintain restraint and respect one another’s activities.

item.title: Journalist shot dead in Netrokona
item.description:
A journalist was shot dead by unidentified assailants while sitting at a shop in Netrokona’s Durgapur upazila on Thursday night.
The victim, Lutfuzzaman Alif Fakir, was the Netrokona correspondent for private IPTV channel Ruposhi Bangla. He also ran a Facebook page titled “Detective Article”, where he wrote about alleged irregularities and crimes.
The attack took place around 8:15pm at Utrail Bazar on the Shyamganj-Birishiri Road in Kolmakanda municipality.
According to eyewitnesses and police, Alif was sitting at a shop when two men arrived on a motorcycle and fired several shots at him before fleeing the scene.
Locals rushed him to the upazila health complex, where an on-duty doctor declared him dead.
Durgapur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Khandkar Shaker Ahmed Khan said five bullet wounds were found on different parts of Alif’s body, including his head, neck and chest.
Netrokona Superintendent of Police Md Tarikul Islam, who was heading to the scene after learning of the killing, said that police initially suspected it was a planned murder.
Police were conducting operations to arrest those involved, he added.
Alif’s ancestral home is in Sunai village of Pogla union in Kolmakanda upazila.
He had previously been attacked on November 10 last year near the Teribazar ferry ghat on the Someshwari River in the same upazila.
Assailants had hacked him, while a colleague who tried to intervene was threatened with a weapon and chased away.

item.title: From Ismat Chughtai to Dhaka airport: Trapped in the moral policing of the 1940s
item.description:
The recent incident involving the alleged imposition of “male guardianship” on three adult women at Dhaka’s international airport is deeply troubling.
The three friends were barred from boarding a flight to Kathmandu for a holiday after immigration officials subjected them to intrusive questioning, moral policing, and harassment.
All three had valid passports, visas, and airline tickets, with no known legal or travel restrictions. Yet, immigration officers stopped them at the checkpoint, interrogated them about their personal lives, and ultimately prevented them from travelling.
What kind of archaic moral policing are we practicing to curtail young women’s freedom of movement in the 21st century?
Fortunately, the incident did not go unchallenged. Forced to miss their scheduled flight, the women refused to let the matter rest and are now pursuing legal action.
This kind of social intrusion and incivility brings to mind a short story I read during my school years in the 1970s.
Written in the early 1940s by Ismat Chughtai, one of the subcontinent’s finest Urdu storytellers, the story is titled Ek Shauhar Ki Khatir (All for a Husband). Although written nearly a century ago, its plot bears an unsettling resemblance to the recent incident at Dhaka airport, highlighting how little our society has changed.
Chughtai’s story revolves around a young, educated, unmarried woman who decides to travel alone by train across British India. Despite warnings from friends and relatives that travelling unescorted is dangerous and socially unacceptable, she sets off on her journey.
En route from Jodhpur to Bombay, she encounters passengers from different walks of life who are deeply unsettled by her decision to travel alone. Her fellow passengers, particularly the traditionally-minded women in the carriage, display palpable patriarchal anxiety over her safety, mobility, and lack of a male protector.
Initially, the train compartment was relatively empty. But as more passengers board, her peaceful journey turns into a battle of intrusive questions.
Her fellow travellers immediately begin probing into her personal life: Where is she going -- to her parents’ home or her husband’s? Where is her husband? Why is she travelling alone? When she casually reveals that she is unmarried and is not going to her parents’ home, their suspicion gives way to pity and horror. To the traditional women in the carriage, an unmarried woman of her age travelling alone is a social anomaly that must somehow be corrected.
To escape their scrutiny and navigate their absurd social expectations, the protagonist decides to play along, claiming that she is married. But the interrogation continues.
Her fellow passengers then demand to know how many children she has. Matching the absurdity of their worldview with equally absurd fabrications, she begins spinning increasingly implausible tales.
When one passenger calculates the timeline and questions how she could have had eight children in just four years of marriage, the protagonist retorts that it is entirely possible to have triplets or quadruplets at a time.
Through the seemingly ordinary setting of a moving train compartment, Chughtai brilliantly satirizes society’s attempts to force independent women into rigid domestic roles. The story draws a timeless parallel with the physical and institutional checkpoints women continue to face today.
Nearly a century later, young, unmarried women in our part of the world continue to face the same patriarchal surveillance, restrictions and moral policing.
Consider an incident in May 2013, when a case at Mumbai’s international airport in India attracted widespread public attention. A 21-year-old female student planning to backpack alone across Europe was subjected to an aggressive and intrusive interrogation by an immigration officer who demanded to know why she was travelling alone.
Crossing all professional boundaries, the officer reportedly said that if her parents allowed her to backpack alone, her family background was “questionable.” He also warned her not to “go crying to the embassy” if anything went wrong.
The ensuing public outcry prompted the Bureau of Immigration to remove the officer from frontline duties permanently and introduce mandatory gender-sensitization workshops at major Indian airports.
Yet, here we are in late 2026, witnessing similar allegations of institutional overreach at Dhaka airport. The officers reportedly questioned why the three women were unmarried, why they were travelling without a male guardian, and whether their families had given them “permission” to travel.
They allegedly went so far as to call one woman’s father and subject him to a humiliating conversation. When challenged, the officials reportedly failed to provide any legal explanation or written justification for stopping the women, effectively derailing their trip.
It is heartening that the travellers refused to remain silent. After their initial administrative complaints went unanswered, they filed a writ petition. In late September 2026, a High Court bench issued a rule questioning the legality of the immigration officials’ actions and asking the home secretary and immigration authorities to explain why preventing adult women from travelling on the basis of their marital or guardianship status should not be declared illegal.
Some officials have informally sought to justify such intrusive questioning by citing the risk of human trafficking through air travel. But can egregious moral policing be excused in the name of anti-trafficking measures? Absolutely not.
Anti-trafficking protocols must never be weaponized to justify gender-based discrimination. A legitimate security mandate does not give officials licence to make offensive remarks about women passengers’ attire, scrutinize their personal finances without proper grounds, or change their professional conduct based solely on a passenger’s marital status.
In Ek Shauhar Ki Khatir , the moment the protagonist assumes the socially sanctioned identity of a “wife,” she is suddenly considered safe and acceptable. The episode exposes just how superficial and arbitrary these social boundaries are.
Nearly a century later, we must ask our state institutions: Do officials manning our international borders really expect unmarried women travelling alone to lie about their marital status and invent male guardians simply to clear immigration?
Unless we dismantle this institutionalized moral policing, our state apparatus will remain little different from the regressive, gossiping train compartment of the 1940s: Frozen in time, hostile to progress, and profoundly threatened by the sight of an independent woman.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: Reclaiming our right to breathe
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s characterization of Dhaka’s persistent toxic air as a “matter of national shame” is the sort of candid admission we would like to see more of.
Acknowledging that poisoning the air our children breathe is a deep institutional and civic failure is the vital first step toward addressing the challenge.
For years, our capital’s routine ranking at the very top of global hazardous air quality indexes was met by successive administrations with bureaucratic shrugs, passing the blame to seasonal weather pattern changes, or issuing advisory notices which had little to no substance. This has only exacerbated the air pollution crisis we find ourselves in today.
However, recognizing national embarrassment must immediately be followed by aggressive, uncompromising state action.
While we cannot control every factor that contributes to our toxic air quality, the primary culprits behind Dhaka’s suffocating smog are well-documented: Uncoordinated and unmonitored construction projects kicking up dust, thousands of unfit, smoke-belching vehicles plying the roads and highways, and brick kilns operating around the capital’s periphery in complete defiance of laws and environmental regulations.
The result has been a public health disaster costing thousands of lives annually and draining billions from our healthcare economy.
The PM’s call for public officials to go beyond routine "nine-to-five" duties and take ownership of environmental protection must be heeded. The Ministry of Environment, Forest, and Climate Change, alongside other relevant authority bodies, can no longer treat pollution control as an afterthought.
Addressing Dhaka's air quality requires a zero tolerance approach, which begins with those in power actually caring enough to work on it seriously. Words of acknowledgment are a welcome departure from past denial but will prove to be meaningless if the state does not back those words to reclaim our right to breathe.

item.title: Taking a hard stance against construction oversights
item.description:
The tragic collapse of roof shuttering at an under-construction municipal building in Pirganj, Rangpur - which claimed the lives of two workers and left several others injured - is yet another incident that shows Bangladesh’s broken construction oversight.
Day after day, day labourers risk their lives on sites where elementary structural safety measures are routinely sacrificed to cut costs and accelerate deadlines. That this fatal disaster occurred on a public municipal site built under the auspices of the local government makes the negligence all the more indefensible, although, regrettably, not surprising.
In the immediate aftermath, law enforcement have detained the municipal secretary of Pirganj. While preliminary administrative detentions signal initial action, we have seen that all too frequently, high-profile construction disasters end with low-level officials or site supervisors scapegoated to appease public outrage, while influential individuals and decision-makers walk away untouched.
A superficial investigation will not suffice, not for this particular incident nor for future ones. We require a rigorous, independent technical probe to uncover the root causes of this collapse.
Law enforcement must ensure that everyone responsible be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law, regardless of their political connections or administrative rank.
This is far from an isolated incident; structural collapses, fallen scaffolding, and unprotected worksites remain a recurring issue across our country. Construction work must not continue to be a death sentence for vulnerable labourers earning daily wages.
We must enforce strict workplace safety standards, conduct site audits, and impose severe criminal penalties on negligence to begin correcting this issue. Until accountability reaches the very top, human lives will continue to be treated as cheap collateral on our building sites.

item.title: Controlling dengue requires a national strategy rooted in One Health
item.description:
Dengue in Bangladesh is no longer a temporary or seasonal health inconvenience; it has evolved into a persistent, multi-faceted public health crisis and a heavy burden on the national economy.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) dengue dashboard, over 107,000 individuals have been hospitalized, and more than 331 deaths have been officially documented as of October 15, 2026. With approximately 2,000 new patients admitted daily, the strain on the healthcare system is overwhelming.
Major tertiary hospitals in Dhaka and urban hubs are facing severe shortages of hospital beds and intensive care unit (ICU) capacities. Relatives face frantic scrambles for blood platelets, revealing the systemic fragility of urban medical infrastructure.
These alarming conditions highlight a critical truth: Reactive clinical management after people fall ill, paired with ad-hoc vector control drives, cannot control the transmission chain.
What Bangladesh urgently requires is a year-round, evidence-based preventive policy anchored in a coordinated national framework.
The uninterrupted spread of dengue is deeply intertwined with climate change, unplanned rapid urbanization, chronic waterlogging, and inadequate municipal waste management.
Global environmental and epidemiological research demonstrates that climate volatility, characterized by rising mean temperatures, erratic unseasonal precipitation, and elevated atmospheric humidity, dramatically accelerates the breeding cycles and vector efficiency of Aedes mosquitoes.
Under higher ambient temperatures, the duration required for the dengue virus to replicate inside the mosquito and reach its salivary glands, is significantly shortened. Consequently, an infected female Aedes mosquito becomes capable of transmitting the pathogen to human hosts much faster and more frequently within its lifespan.
Concurrently, urban environments proliferate with artificial micro-habitats. Construction sites, poorly designed drainage infrastructure, discarded single-use plastics, and poorly maintained rooftop gardens collect stagnant water, offering ideal breeding conditions.
Relying exclusively on hospital-centred curative care to address what is inherently an environmental and eco-climatic phenomenon is inherently flawed.
For decades, vector control efforts in Bangladesh have remained stubbornly reactive. Intervention plans are typically mobilized only after hospital admissions surge to crisis levels, taking the form of temporary fogging drives or hospital bed expansions.
Yet, such reactive measures fail to answer fundamental operational questions:
Indiscriminate fogging without routine entomological monitoring wastes municipal resources and damages urban ecosystems, killing beneficial non-target insects while accelerating insecticide resistance in Aedes vectors.
Transitioning from reactive fogging to sustainable vector management demands source reduction, routine larvicidal suppression, systematic waste removal, and targeted bio-control methods.
In this complex landscape, the 'One Health' framework offers the most viable path forward. One Health is an integrated, unifying approach that recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human health, animal health, and the shared environment.
While dengue is not directly transmitted from animals to humans, it is a vector-borne viral disease reliant on the interaction between human hosts, viral pathogens, mosquito vectors, and ambient environmental conditions.
Applying One Health to dengue control means treating vector ecology, climatic dynamics, human mobility, and urban sanitation as a single interconnected ecosystem.
It breaks down traditional administrative silos, bringing together public health physicians, specialists, medical entomologists, environmental scientists, climate researchers, urban planners, and municipal engineers onto a unified operational platform.
The government recently formed a high-level special taskforce comprising representatives across various ministries and authorities to oversee mosquito-borne disease management, a commendable administrative step.
However, to translate policy into measurable health outcomes, this taskforce must move beyond administrative governance and actively embed the One Health framework into its operational core, with entomologists, climate specialists, and One Health practitioners needing to hold direct scientific advisory roles.
Crucially, Bangladesh needs a predictive national early warning and surveillance system that synthesizes real-time meteorological forecasts, rainfall patterns, vector density indices, larval mapping, and clinical hospitalization data.
Analyzing these spatial data streams will allow authorities to forecast outbreak clusters weeks before human cases spike, shifting intervention efforts from reactive crisis management to pre-emptive prevention.
Academic institutions and research centres must also be integrated into local intervention trials to evaluate the efficacy of eco-friendly larvicides and biological vector suppression tools tailored to micro-climatic zones.
Community participation remains vital to sustaining these interventions. Public awareness campaigns must empower citizens to inspect their surroundings, eliminate standing water, dispose of water-retaining trash, and neutralize mosquito breeding sites around homes.
However, civic responsibility must not serve as an excuse for institutional inaction. Local municipal authorities bear the primary obligation to ensure reliable solid waste collection, maintain open drainage canals, prevent waterlogging, and enforce environmental compliance across urban construction projects.
Controlling dengue demands a departure from fragmented, seasonal measures in favour of a long-term, science-driven, and accountable national strategy.
Clinical preparedness must be balanced with environmental management, integrated surveillance, and robust inter-ministerial coordination.
Ultimately, the success of national dengue control must not be measured by how many hospital beds are arranged to treat the sick, but by how many infections are prevented, how many vector breeding sites are permanently eliminated, and how many lives are protected.
Without a structural transition to a One Health paradigm, Bangladesh will remain trapped in a recurring cycle of preventable loss of life and severe economic strain year after year.
Professor Dr KBM Saiful Islam is the former Dean of the Faculty of Animal Science & Veterinary Medicine and former Chairman of the Department of Medicine & Public Health at Sher‑e‑Bangla Agricultural University. He previously served as a member of the National Coordination Committee of One Health Bangladesh.

item.title: Vikings to celebrate 30 years with album and film
item.description:
Bangladeshi rock band Vikings will celebrate its 30th anniversary in 2027 with a new album and a 45-minute film, both titled “Vikings Replayed.”
The album, scheduled for release on January 1, 2027, will feature reworked versions of 11 songs from the band’s first two albums. The film is expected to follow about a week later.
The band has yet to reveal the tracklist. Vocalist and band leader Tonmoy Tansen said the selection would remain a surprise for listeners.
The project aims to introduce the band’s earlier music to younger audiences while reconnecting longtime fans with the songs.
“We have a generation of listeners who grew up with these songs, but musical tastes and technology have changed considerably since then,” Tansen said. “We wanted to preserve the connection with our older audience while also making the songs accessible to Gen Z. The sound will be quite different, with contemporary technology playing an important part in the new arrangements.”
Vikings released its debut album, “Jiboner Kolahol,” in 2000, followed by “Din Joto Dukkho Toto” in 2002. The band returned with “Run Out” in 2015, an album featuring 6 songs composed for Tansen’s film of the same name.
The upcoming film will document the band’s journey from its early days to the present, featuring memories, relationships, challenges, and milestones from its career.
The project began taking shape during a 15-day stay at Ocean Paradise Hotel in Cox’s Bazar in September 2025. The band worked on initial arrangements for the reimagined songs while filming portions of the movie.
Tansen, who previously directed “Run Out” and “Padma Patar Jol,” was familiar with filmmaking. For the other band members, acting and participating in the production offered a new experience.
“We are used to making music, but turning that journey into a film meant thinking about dialogue and acting as well,” Tansen said. “It was a completely different experience for all of us.”
Vikings has been less active on stage since 2024 as it focused on the album and film. Tansen hopes the projects will help the band return to live performances with renewed momentum.
Following “Vikings Replayed,” the band plans to begin work on a new album of original songs.

item.title: Houthis launch deadly attack on presidential palace in Yemen’s Aden
item.description:
The Houthis launched a deadly missile attack Thursday on the presidential palace in the Yemeni government’s interim capital of Aden, as Saudi Arabia blamed Iran for the recent dramatic escalation in the long-running war.
Saudi Arabia and the internationally recognized government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained Houthi attack of late, shifting the focus of the wider Middle East war that erupted with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February.
The Iran-backed Houthis have seized swathes of territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline in recent weeks, and a government counteroffensive with Saudi air support has so far failed to reverse the gains.
Government military sources in Yemen said at least four people were killed and 10 wounded in Thursdays strikes on Adens Al-Maashiq palace, which also serves as the government’s headquarters in the divided country’s south.
An AFP journalist saw smoke rising and residents of the southern city reported hearing explosions during the attack, the first on the complex since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
Yemeni information minister Moammar al-Eryani said the prime minister and cabinet ministers were safe, adding the attack had been carried out with five missiles.
A government minister said on condition of anonymity that Prime Minister Shaya al-Zindani had been present at the time, but “was not harmed in any way.”
Media affiliated with the Houthis said they had targeted “the headquarters of military operations, led by Saudi officers, at the Al-Maashiq Palace in Aden, as well as weapons depots belonging to them.”
Yemen’s civil war -- in which Saudi Arabia has led a military coalition supporting the government since 2015 -- reignited after the collapse of a years-long truce, with the Houthis going on to launch their lightning offensive in September.
Riyadh on Thursday accused Iran of encouraging the escalation, saying it continued to arm and train the group.
Saudi Arabia’s deputy minister for public diplomacy at the foreign ministry said Riyadh was still in touch with Iran, but that Tehran did not appear ready to make concessions.
“We think that the escalation by the Houthis at this latest stage of the conflict is encouraged by Iran,” said Dr Rayed Krimly.
The Saudi-led coalition said drones fired by the Houthis at the kingdom’s southern region and the city of Khamis Mushait were intercepted.
Yemeni government forces said the Houthis had also fired “several ballistic missiles” at the central city of Marib, which sits in a strategic oil-rich region.
In 2023, regional rivals Iran and Saudi Arabia reached a deal mediated by China to thaw a longstanding freeze in ties, but the latest violence might threaten to upend the entente.
The Saudi ministry official went on to accuse the Houthis of refusing to meet as fighting ramped up between the two sides.
“At the beginning of this escalation, we asked them to meet in Muscat, Oman and they refused,” he added.
The ministry later said that the exchange took place in July.
Saudi Arabia suffered its deadliest attack in more than a decade on Saturday when a strike on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded around 300 others.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said the group had attacked Riyadh’s airport 20 times this month.
Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said “The Houthis must immediately cease all terrorist operations targeting civilians and civilian facilities, including airports, ports, oil facilities, and infrastructure.”
He added the group had “worked to obtain advanced technologies with the help of regional actors,” saying they now had “ballistic missiles, attack and suicide drones, and fast explosive-laden boats.”
The attacks on Saudi Arabia have tested the country’s infrastructure and resilience, the energy minister acknowledged earlier this week.
Riyadh usually hosts a packed calendar of events this time of year, including its flagship investment conference drawing foreign leaders and business titans.
In Yemen, the conflict has caused what the United Nations calls one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, leaving most of the nation’s population dependent on aid.
